Amazingly Clean 1973 Pontiac GTO Is a One-Year-Only Gem
12 photos
Photo: That Muscle car guy/YouTube
Introduced in 1964 as an option package on the LeMans, the Pontiac GTO is credited with having kickstarted the muscle car craze. It remained highly popular until 1971, when sales dropped to only 10,532 units. The nameplate was discontinued in 1974, with the final-year model being a package on the compact Ventura.
Pontiac sold three different generations of the GTO. The first one lasted from 1964 to 1967, with a notable redesign introduced in 1965. The second-gen model, produced from 1968 to 1972, got a significant overhaul in 1970. Finally, the third-generation GTO was produced for one single year, 1973.
The latter was also an option package for the LeMans and featured GM's Colonnade body, which eliminated the authentic hardtop design. Unlike its predecessor, it also featured prominent chrome bumpers, which were added due to then-new federal laws. The 1973 GTO was not well received by the public, with sales hitting an all-time low of 4,806 units.
The 1973 GTO is obviously the least desirable iteration of the series. Because of this, many cars are still rotting away in junkyards and barns. Pristine survivors are super rare, while restored examples are hard to come by. This silver Sport Coupe is one of those lucky examples that got a second chance and looks fresh despite being 53 years old as of 2026.
Although its design doesn't get a lot of love, I actually like the 1973 GTO. I'm a big fan of the V-shaped hood that extends into the upper side panels, the muscular rear fenders, and the flat, almost boat-tail-like rear end. The silver paint also suits this body style quite well, and the burgundy interior makes for a striking contrast.
There's no info as to when this GTO was restored, but it looks pretty much flawless inside and out. Our host doesn't open the hood but confirms that the Poncho packs a 400-cubic-inch (6.6-liter) V8 engine.
This was the standard unit in 1973. Pontiac reduced the compression ratio to 8.0:1, and oomph dropped to 230 horsepower. An optional 455-cubic-inch (7.5-liter) V8 was available with 250 horsepower. The 455 HO unit was discontinued for 1973.
While the 455 unit was exclusively paired with the automatic transmission, the 400 V8 was also offered with manual gearboxes. The three-speed unit was standard, while the four-speed was optional. This GTO was ordered with the latter.
The three-pedal layout makes this GTO pretty rare. Existing records from PHS show that only 1,113 units were equipped with the manual transmission. The figure includes 187 Coupes and 926 Sport Coupes. This GTO is a Sport Coupe. These figures are for both three- and four-speed manual cars, but the former is pretty uncommon.
The color combo could also be described as uncommon. That's mainly because the burgundy interior was only available with five exterior colors, with Ascot Silver being one of them. I'd say that fewer than 100 examples were built exactly like this. What's your take on the 1973 GTO ? Would you drive one?
